Choosing a model

Source: vignettes/choosing-a-model.Rmd
choosing-a-model.Rmd
library(decisions)

Overview

Different providers host different decision models. The decisions package gives them one interface. So you can run the same question with each model and compare the results.

This vignette compares three models on one text task:

  • Jev, from TypeSafe, with decider_typesafe().
  • Microsoft-Decision-1, through OpenRouter, with decider_openrouter().
  • The Decisions API of OpenAI, with decider_openai(). Its default model is gpt-6-luna.

The results below come from live calls. The package saved them in inst/extdata, so this vignette builds without a key and without a network. The code that made them is in data-raw/vignette_results.R.

Credentials

Each provider has its own key. decide() reads the key from an environment variable when it sends the requests, as ellmer does.

Provider Decider Environment variable
TypeSafe decider_typesafe() TYPESAFE_API_KEY
OpenRouter decider_openrouter() OPENROUTER_API_KEY
OpenAI decider_openai() OPENAI_API_KEY

Set the variables in ~/.Renviron, then restart R. A decider holds no key. Each decider also takes a credentials function that returns the key. The function replaces the environment variable.

Data

The package has the dataset ohio_injuries. It has the narratives of 464 severe work injuries in Ohio. The source is the Severe Injury Reports of the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). The column collapsed_nature_title has five injury types: amputation, fracture, crushing injury, thermal burn and concussion. See ?ohio_injuries for the details.

Source:

Occupational Safety and Health Administration. (n.d.). Severe injury reports [Data set]. U.S. Department of Labor. Retrieved October 23, 2026, from https://www.osha.gov/severe-injury-reports

We used the filters Year: 2025 and State: Ohio.

For context: the NIOSH Center for Workers’ Compensation Studies reports the claim counts and rates of the Ohio Bureau of Workers’ Compensation (https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/worker-comp/about/index.html).

The five groups differ in size: 187 amputations and 242 fractures, but only 14 crushing injuries, 15 thermal burns and 6 concussions. We take all the reports of the three small groups and 20 reports of each large group. The seed is fixed. This gives 75 narratives.

set.seed(2026)
injuries <- ohio_injuries |>
  dplyr::slice_sample(n = 20, by = collapsed_nature_title)

dplyr::count(injuries, collapsed_nature_title)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   collapsed_nature_title     n
#>   <fct>                  <int>
#> 1 amputation                20
#> 2 fracture                  20
#> 3 crushing injury           14
#> 4 thermal burn              15
#> 5 concussion                 6

The truth is the column collapsed_nature_title, a factor. Its levels are the five injury types, in the order above.

Question

One choice question has the five injury types as its answers. The descriptions are general. The model reads the narrative of each report.

nature <- question_choice(
  "Which injury does this report of a work injury describe? Choose the main injury.",
  c(
    amputation = "A body part is cut or torn off, in whole or in part.",
    fracture = "A bone is broken or cracked.",
    `crushing injury` = "A body part is squeezed hard between objects, and the tissue is damaged.",
    `thermal burn` = "Heat, flame, hot liquid or a hot surface burns the skin.",
    concussion = "A blow or a shake to the head hurts the brain."
  )
)

Three models

purrr::map() runs decide() once for each decider. One call of decide() uses one model. The list deciders is named, so the list of answers is named too.

deciders <- list(
  jev = decider_typesafe(),
  microsoft = decider_openrouter("microsoft/microsoft-decision-1"),
  openai = decider_openai()
)

answers <- purrr::map(deciders, \(decider) decide(decider, nature, text = injuries$final_narrative))

Each element of answers is a tibble with 75 rows, in the order of the narratives. We bind the three tibbles and add the truth.

results <- answers |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "model") |>
  dplyr::mutate(truth = rep(injuries$collapsed_nature_title, times = length(answers)))

The levels of .pred_class are the five answers, as in truth. A name with a space gives a probability column with a clean name: crushing injury gives .pred_crushing_injury.

grep("^\\.pred_", names(results), value = TRUE)
#> [1] ".pred_class"           ".pred_amputation"      ".pred_fracture"        ".pred_crushing_injury"
#> [5] ".pred_thermal_burn"    ".pred_concussion"

Performance

yardstick reads the columns that decide() returns. accuracy() compares truth with .pred_class. roc_auc() takes the five probability columns, in the order of the levels of truth. With more than two classes, it computes the multiclass ROC AUC of Hand and Till.

metrics <- yardstick::metric_set(yardstick::accuracy, yardstick::roc_auc)

results |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  metrics(
    truth,
    .pred_amputation, .pred_fracture, .pred_crushing_injury, .pred_thermal_burn, .pred_concussion,
    estimate = .pred_class
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(model, .metric, .estimate)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   model     .metric  .estimate
#>   <chr>     <chr>        <dbl>
#> 1 jev       accuracy     0.96 
#> 2 microsoft accuracy     0.947
#> 3 openai    accuracy     0.987
#> 4 jev       roc_auc      1    
#> 5 microsoft roc_auc      1    
#> 6 openai    roc_auc      1

A row with an error has NA answers, and yardstick removes it. The table shows how many rows each model answered.

results |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(rows = dplyr::n(), errors = sum(!is.na(.error)))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   model      rows errors
#>   <chr>     <int>  <int>
#> 1 jev          75      0
#> 2 microsoft    75      0
#> 3 openai       75      0

The confusion matrix of each model shows the counts. The rows are the answers of the model, and the columns are the truth.

results |>
  split(results$model) |>
  purrr::map(\(x) yardstick::conf_mat(x, truth, .pred_class)$table)
#> $jev
#>                  Truth
#> Prediction        amputation fracture crushing injury thermal burn concussion
#>   amputation              19        0               0            0          0
#>   fracture                 0       20               0            0          1
#>   crushing injury          1        0              14            1          0
#>   thermal burn             0        0               0           14          0
#>   concussion               0        0               0            0          5
#> 
#> $microsoft
#>                  Truth
#> Prediction        amputation fracture crushing injury thermal burn concussion
#>   amputation              17        0               0            0          0
#>   fracture                 0       20               0            0          0
#>   crushing injury          3        0              14            1          0
#>   thermal burn             0        0               0           14          0
#>   concussion               0        0               0            0          6
#> 
#> $openai
#>                  Truth
#> Prediction        amputation fracture crushing injury thermal burn concussion
#>   amputation              20        0               0            0          0
#>   fracture                 0       20               0            0          1
#>   crushing injury          0        0              14            0          0
#>   thermal burn             0        0               0           15          0
#>   concussion               0        0               0            0          5

All three models do well on this task, and their scores differ by a few reports. Seventy-five narratives and small groups give a rough comparison only. The group concussion has 6 reports, so one report changes its share by 17 points. Use more rows before you choose a model for real work.

Cost and time

Each provider reports different things. OpenRouter reports the cost of each call. TypeSafe and OpenAI report none, so .cost is NA for them, and decide() prints one message about it. All three report the input tokens. .seconds is the time of one response. The requests run in parallel, so these times do not add up to the time of the whole call.

results |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    input_tokens = sum(.input_tokens, na.rm = TRUE),
    cost_usd = if (all(is.na(.cost))) NA_real_ else sum(.cost, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_seconds = median(.seconds, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   model     input_tokens  cost_usd median_seconds
#>   <chr>            <dbl>     <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 jev              36122 NA                0.0908
#> 2 microsoft        12885  0.000541         0.192 
#> 3 openai           18670 NA                0.156

The prices of the providers differ. To compare the cost, take the input tokens and the price list of each provider.
